extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Renaissance literature and legal satire (Rabelais scholars, general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter excerpt from Rabelais (legal-satirical prose) describing purported judicial practices and legal maxims in a comic/illustrative narrative voice. Useful for literary analysis or study of satirical treatments of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excuse for infirmity (physical incapacity as non-culpatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the imperfections of nature should never be imputed unto any for crimes and transgressions” (used to excuse old age and dim sight when judging).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat natural infirmities (age, failing sight) as mitigating/exculpatory factors; do not impute them as criminal faults. The narrator cites canonical authorities to justify leniency for personal imperfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alea Judiciorum — use of chance in final determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to the dice of sentences at law, Alea Judiciorum, and the narrator’s practice of deciding some suits by the 'chance and throw of the dice'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As presented (satirically), judges may resort to aleatory methods for final disposition when customary; the text cites legal glosses and authorities that purportedly validate the use of chance to close disputes when applied as customary practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor the defendant when rights are obscure
rubrics_metrics.description: “Quum sunt partium jura obscura, reo potius favendum est quam actori.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the rights of the parties are obscure or law is ambiguous, prefer the defendant (favor the accused/lesser claimant). The passage treats this as an established maxim to resolve doubtful cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the minimum in obscurities (Semper in obscuris quod minimum est sequimur)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Semper in obscuris quod minimum est sequimur” — in obscurities follow what is least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases of uncertainty, choose the lesser (minimal) option; linked in the narrative to judges’ customary practice of selecting the smaller/lesser interpretation in unclear situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict adherence to formalities (form is decisive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalities are necessary: omission makes acts 'of no force nor value' — 'for formality sake, the omission whereof ... is excellently well proved'. Also invoked: 'Forma mutata, mutatur substantia.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural and formal requirements are decisive; failure to observe formalities can void substantive rights. The text emphasizes that forms give legal being ('forma dat esse') and that changing form alters substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough documentary review before decision
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge ought to have 'well and exactly seen, surveyed, overlooked, reviewed, recognized, read ... the bills of complaint, accusations, impeachments, indictments, ... depositions, cross speeches, contradictions ...' etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comprehensive examination of all pleadings, documents, evidence, and procedural papers is required (or at least prescribed in the narrative) before adjudication; the long list functions as guidance for exhaustive procedural review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use different 'dice' sizes depending on case clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bridlegoose claims 'I have other large great dice ... which I employ ... when the matter is more plain, clear, and liquid ... But when there are many bags on the one side and on the other, I then use my little small dice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a rule-of-thumb (satirical): employ a 'small dice' (more granular/random rule) for complex, contested matters with many papers; use 'large dice' when matters are plain and few. The passage frames this as customary judicial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow judicial recreation/exercise as necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of recreative exercises (games) is allowed to officers of justice: 'the practice of such-like exercitations is appointed to be laid hold on by your other worships, and consequently not to be denied unto me.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recreation and physical exercise for judges/officials are defended as healthful and appropriate; the narrator cites physicians and legal glosses to justify leisure activities as part of a judge’s life (satirical normative claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defer judgment until the matter ripens (time as father of truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time ripeneth and bringeth all things to maturity; the narrator defers, 'protract, delay, prolong... the time of giving a definitive sentence' so the suit may be 'well fanned and winnowed' and parties better endure the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay is endorsed as a judicial technique: letting a case mature yields clearer truth, reduces rancour, and produces more patient acceptance of outcomes. The text lists many verbs of postponement to stress intentional temporal management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature decrees (wait for cases to be 'ripe')
rubrics_metrics.description: A decree passed when action is 'raw, crude, green, unripe' is dangerous — compared to piercing an imposthume before it be ripe; one should act when full maturity is reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resolve matters at an early stage; like physicians and harvesters, legal actors should wait for proper maturation before decisive intervention to avoid harm or error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case completeness judged by accumulation of papers ('forma dat esse')
rubrics_metrics.description: A suit at its beginning is 'shapeless' and 'without form'; when there are heaps of papers 'packed, piled ... put up in bags' then the suit may be termed 'well-formed and fashioned' — 'forma dat esse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative equates procedural completeness and legitimacy with voluminous documentary apparatus: a well-documented case is treated as fully formed and proper for adjudication; this functions as an implicit metric for case readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic timing for reconciliation (intervene when parties are exhausted)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reconcilers (e.g., Peter Dandin) succeed by taking parties 'at that very instant nick of time when both those of the one and the other side should be weary and tired' and 'when they had voided and emptied their own cashes and coffers'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mediators should choose moments when disputants are financially or emotionally spent to encourage agreement; the narrator presents late intervention as the pragmatic method for securing reconciliations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalized procedural layering before final disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: In criminal cases Bridlegoose permits departure, requires sleep, a report and attestation of sleep, issues a warrant to convene, then successive acts are produced — 'consopiating act engendereth another act' until the process is 'completely well formed and perfect in all his members' before resorting to dice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial procedure should progress through formalized, linked acts that build the process incrementally; only after this chain of formal steps is the final disposition (satirically, even by chance) applied.
